title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
This site documents one repository that contains two packages. They are developed, tested and released together. The division between them is the following:
Storage, indexing and search are implemented in the engine. The server calls the engine’s public API and does not use its internal modules. The engine contains no reference to HTTP status codes or to process exit codes.
This separation determines how failures are reported. The engine raises a typed error, and the category of that error states the nature of the failure. Each interface then maps the category to its own vocabulary: HTTP status codes, command-line exit codes, or a branch in a Julia program.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
What it gives you

Project lifecycle: create_project, open_project, close_project! manage a project’s on-disk RocksDB directory and the live search engine backing it.
A project says what it holds, and separately what holds it: engine= is DenseEngine, SparseEngine or FullTextEngine — dense vectors, sparse vectors, text — and backend= is the index underneath it, defaulting to that engine’s own (SearchGraph, InvertedFile, BM25InvertedFile). payload_kind(engine) answers the first question for a project you opened; BACKENDS lists the legal pairings.
Dense vector search over a SearchGraph (an approximate, self-tuning graph index), or an exact ExhaustiveSearch/ParallelExhaustiveSearch, all sharing the same append_items!/search surface — for a SearchGraph, append_items! only stages raw vectors, and the (expensive) graph-connection step happens in a separate, explicit index! call, so a caller controls when that cost is paid.
Sparse vector search over an InvertedFile, for vectors you encoded — a learned sparse retriever, a feature table, a set of ids. It takes SparseItems of a dimension fixed at creation, under any distance that reads a sparse vector (cosine over the weights, or one of Dist.Sets.* over the nonzero positions), and there is no vocabulary, no profile and no tokenizer anywhere in it. BM25 is deliberately not among its distances: it scores from corpus statistics rather than from a vector, so it belongs to a text project.
Full-text search, where this package does the encoding, over a BM25InvertedFile or a weighted TextInvertedFile, sharing the same append_items!(stage)/index!(build)/ftsearch surface as the dense case — the first index! call on a text project also fits its TextProfile from whatever’s been staged so far, so there’s no separate training step to call first.
A text model stated explicitly: creating a text project requires a textmodel, and there is no default. Prefer DefaultProfile(:es) — the published profile for a language, refitted to your own corpus at the first index! call, so your weights are calibrated over millions of paragraphs and the stopwords, lemmas and query-expansion network are inherited rather than derived (refit=false keeps the base’s language-wide vocabulary instead). BaseProfile(p) uses a profile you already hold. FitFromCorpus(TextConfig(language=:es)) is the explicit “no base profile” escape, delegated to TextSearch.fit_profile and capped at max_documents to bound its cost — which makes its vocabulary thin, and that is not a decision to arrive at by omission. Queries then travel with a QueryPolicy: whether to correct their spelling against the vocabulary (ftexplain reports what was corrected, correction=:off undoes it) and whether to widen them with the profile’s expansion network.
Typed in, typed out: items are DenseItem/SparseItem/TextItem values and results are SearchResult/StoredItem/ExistsResult. No JSON-shaped dictionary is taken apart by key name on the way in or assembled on the way out; meta stays a free-form Dict{String,Any}, and get_raw_meta is the one raw path, reserved for the HTTP server.
Soft deletes: delete_item! marks a document as logically deleted without touching the underlying index; search reports a deleted marker per candidate instead of silently hiding or backfilling it.
Recall calibration: calibrate! runs SimilaritySearch.jl’s real hyperparameter search so later queries can ask for minrecall=0.95 (or any other target) and get back a BeamSearch tuned for it.
Whole-dataset operations: allknn, fft (diverse sampling), closestpairs (near-duplicate detection), and bichromatic_kclosestpairs (closest pairs across two collections) all run synchronously, in-process, against a dense project’s index.
Incremental, per-field persistence: every mutation writes only the storage it actually touched — a SearchGraph’s raw vectors go straight into a memory-mapped file, a soft delete never rewrites the index, and routine inserts never rewrite the whole engine state. See Architecture for the on-disk layout.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Where this fits
This package is deliberately scoped to project lifecycle, core CRUD, calibration, and the whole-dataset operations (allknn, fft, closestpairs, bichromatic_kclosestpairs).
It has two kinds of user, and the embedded API is the surface for both. A Julia program does using SimilaritySearchEngine and calls these functions directly — that is a first-class use, not a testing convenience, which is why the API takes and returns typed Julia values rather than JSON-shaped dictionaries. The sibling SimilaritySearchServer is the other: it wraps this same engine in a CLI and an HTTP server, and it is a consumer of this package rather than the reason it exists. Development happens here first, at the engine level, and is ported there afterwards — so a capability can exist here before it has a server counterpart (sparse projects do today), and a project touched through either stays readable by the other, same on-disk layout and same insertion/search/persistence semantics.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Installation
Neither package is registered in the Julia General registry, so both are installed from this repository. The dependencies of the engine are registered: SimilaritySearch.jl, TextSearch.jl, RocksDB.jl, and the RocksDB_jll binaries. No other repository has to be cloned, and the RocksDB binaries are not compiled here:
using Pkg
Pkg.add(url="https://github.com/sadit/SimilaritySearchEngine.jl")
The server is the server/ subdirectory of the same repository, and it resolves the engine by path:
git clone https://github.com/sadit/SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
cd SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
julia --project=server -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.develop(path="."); Pkg.instantiate()'
julia --project=server -t auto -m SimilaritySearchServer serve
Both packages require Julia 1.12 or later. No Manifest.toml is committed for the engine, so Pkg.instantiate() resolves the base libraries from the registry unless they are also developed by path.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Core Capabilities

Project Lifecycle Management: Functions create_project, open_project, and close_project! manage the on-disk RocksDB directory and the associated live search engine.
Engine and Backend Separation:

Payload Engines: DenseEngine, SparseEngine, and FullTextEngine specify the stored data domain.
Index Backends: SearchGraph, ExhaustiveSearch, InvertedFile, and BM25InvertedFile define the underlying indexing data structures.
The function payload_kind(engine) identifies the data domain, and the BACKENDS registry enforces valid engine-backend pairings.

Dense Vector Search: Approximate nearest-neighbor search via SearchGraph with dynamic beam-search tuning, or exact brute-force search via ExhaustiveSearch and ParallelExhaustiveSearch. For SearchGraph, insertions (append_items!) and graph construction (index!) are decoupled to give callers explicit control over indexing latency.
Sparse Vector Search: Native inverted index search (InvertedFile) over user-encoded sparse representations of fixed dimension. Distance functions include cosine distance over weights and discrete set metrics (Dist.Sets.*) over non-zero coordinate supports.
Full-Text Retrieval: Lexical search backed by BM25InvertedFile or TF-IDF-weighted TextInvertedFile. The initial index! call fits or initializes a TextProfile from staged texts, establishing the vocabulary and linguistic weighting model.
Explicit Text Modeling: Text projects require an explicit AbstractTextModelSpec:

DefaultProfile(:lang): Resolves a pre-trained language profile and refits vocabulary frequencies against the staged corpus.
BaseProfile(p): Utilizes an existing, pre-computed TextProfile.
FitFromCorpus(cfg): Fits a new profile directly from the staged corpus, bounded by max_documents.
Query execution accepts a QueryPolicy to control automatic orthographic correction and semantic query expansion.

Strongly Typed Interface: Inputs are encapsulated in typed containers (DenseItem, SparseItem, TextItem), and queries return structured results (SearchResult, StoredItem, ExistsResult).
Logical Deletions: The delete_item! function marks documents as logically deleted without mutating the underlying search index. Queries return candidates alongside an explicit deleted flag.
Target Recall Calibration: The calibrate! function executes hyperparameter optimization to calibrate beam-search configurations for target recall constraints (minrecall).
Whole-Dataset Metric Operations: Synchronous, in-process execution of all-pairs nearest neighbors (allknn), diverse center selection (fft), closest pair discovery (closestpairs), and cross-dataset closest pairs (bichromatic_kclosestpairs).
Granular Storage Persistence: High-throughput persistence utilizing a hybrid layout of RocksDB column families and dedicated memory-mapped vector files (dense_vectors.mmapdb).
Typed Errors: Deliberate failures are raised as EngineError subtypes grouped into four categories (InvalidRequest, NotFound, ConflictingState, StorageFailure), so a caller can act on a failure without interpreting its message.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Ecosystem Role
SimilaritySearchEngine.jl provides the core embedded engine functionality. Higher-level services—HTTP REST APIs, asynchronous job workers, and command-line interfaces—are provided by SimilaritySearchServer, which lives in the same repository under server/ as a separate package with its own dependency set. It consumes this engine’s public API and nothing beneath it; the engine, in turn, knows nothing about HTTP status codes or exit codes.

title: Getting Started
text:
The Reference Dataset: Frankenstein
The test directory contains test/data/frankenstein.jsonl, which provides the complete novel partitioned into 724 paragraphs with metadata annotations:
using JSON

items = [JSON.parse(l) for l in readlines("test/data/frankenstein.jsonl")]
length(items)  # 724 paragraphs
first(keys(items[1]))
Each JSON object defines the following fields: - "text": The raw paragraph string. - "doc_id": An external string identifier (e.g., "frankenstein_1"). - "keywords": Named entities and character names identified in the paragraph (e.g., ["Elizabeth", "Victor"]). - "ref": The doc_id of the preceding paragraph, representing narrative sequence. - "word_count", "verb_count": Arbitrary quantitative metadata stored in the free-form meta JSON dictionary.

title: Getting Started
text:
Dense Vector Search with LSI (SearchGraph)

1. Creating a Dense Project
To initialize a project on disk, call create_project:
using SimilaritySearchEngine

workdir = mktempdir()
h = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense"; engine=DenseEngine, backend=SearchGraph, minrecall=0.9)
The engine keyword specifies the payload domain (DenseEngine), while backend defines the indexing algorithm (SearchGraph).


2. Generating Semantic Embeddings via LSI
To generate continuous vector representations directly from text without external dependencies, we use Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) from TextSearch.jl:
using TextSearch: LatentSemanticIndexing, outdim
using TextSearch.LSI: vectorize

corpus = [it["text"] for it in items]
lsi = LatentSemanticIndexing(corpus; maxoutdim=128, verbose=false)
outdim(lsi)  # 128 dimensions


3. Staging Vector Items
We partition the dataset, appending the first half (362 paragraphs) to the project and reserving the second half for subsequent bichromatic evaluations:
half = length(items) ÷ 2

batch = [
    DenseItem(vectorize(lsi, it["text"]);
              doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"], refs = it["ref"],
              meta = Dict{String,Any}("word_count" => it["word_count"],
                                      "verb_count" => it["verb_count"]))
    for it in items[1:half]
]
append_items!(h, batch)  # Stages 362 vectors into dense_vectors.mmapdb


4. Constructing the Proximity Graph
For a SearchGraph backend, append_items! writes vectors to disk immediately but does not construct graph edges. To build graph connectivity across the staged backlog, invoke index!:
index!(h)  # Builds graph connections over the 362 staged items


5. Executing Queries and Metadata Filtering
Once indexed, queries are evaluated using search:
query = vectorize(lsi, "the monster and its creator")
results = search(h, query, 5)

for r in results
    println("Document ID: ", r.doc_id, " | Distance: ", r.distance)
end
To restrict query evaluation using metadata predicates, pass a filter function (record, meta) -> Bool:
# Filter results to include only paragraphs with non-empty keywords
filtered_results = search(h, query, 5; filter = (record, meta) -> !isempty(record.keywords))
The filter is applied to a fixed number of candidates read from the index. That number is the argument candidates, and its default value is 2k. A filtered search returns fewer than k results when fewer than k of those candidates satisfy the predicate. No error is raised in that case. The alternative behavior, increasing the number of candidates until k results are obtained, would convert a selective predicate into a scan of the entire collection, at two RocksDB reads per candidate.
The value of candidates should correspond to the selectivity of the predicate. A predicate satisfied by approximately one item in \(n\) requires approximately \(n \cdot k\) candidates to return \(k\) results:
# One document in ~26 carries this year: 20 candidates are not enough for 10 results
rare = search(h, query, 10; filter = (record, meta) -> meta["year"] == 2005)                   # returns 0
enough = search(h, query, 10; filter = (record, meta) -> meta["year"] == 2005, candidates=8192) # returns 10


6. Declaring What meta Holds
A project may declare the fields of meta it expects, and the type of each one:
h = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_typed"; engine=DenseEngine, backend=SearchGraph,
                   meta_schema = ["word_count" => :int64, "published" => :timestamp])
append_items! then checks those fields. A value that is not the declared type is rejected with PayloadMismatch; a value that converts without changing is converted, which is what turns the 2024.0 of a JSON document into the integer 2024. Fields that were not declared are stored as they arrive, so declaring is a decision about a few fields rather than about the whole of meta.
What this buys, since the declared fields are not indexed, is that a comparison happens in the declared type. A field declared :timestamp is compared as an instant:
# The same instant written two ways: this matches a record stored as "2026-01-02T00:00:00"
search(h, query, 5; filter = (record, meta) -> Schema.matches_filter(
    record, meta, Dict("published" => "2026-01-02T00:00"), meta_schema(h)))
Declaring on a project that already holds records reads none of them: declare_meta_schema!(h, [...]) governs what is written from then on, and leaves what is stored as it is.


7. Batch Queries
A set of queries is answered in a single parallel pass rather than one call at a time. Passing a vector of query vectors to search returns one result list per query, in the same order:
queries = [vectorize(lsi, t) for t in ["the monster and its creator",
                                       "the arctic expedition",
                                       "letters to Margaret"]]
batched = search(h, queries, 5)     # Vector{Vector{SearchResult}}
batched[2][1].doc_id
searchbatch returns the same neighborhoods without metadata: two matrices of size (k, length(queries)), one of internal identifiers and one of distances. This form is intended for evaluation procedures, offline scoring, and the construction of another index:
ids, dists = searchbatch(h, queries, 5)
size(ids)     # (5, 3)
Measured over 50,000 dense vectors on 8 threads, searchbatch answers 39,000 queries per second, compared with 3,800 queries per second when each query is issued separately. The form that returns metadata answers 12,600 queries per second; the difference is the reading and decoding of the metadata of each result.
Both forms are operations over the entire dataset, not concurrent searches. They acquire the write lock of the project, which excludes other batch calls, and they are rejected while items are staged but not indexed. The reason is their internal parallelism, which cannot be nested under the default thread scheduler. A text project has no batch entry point, because its queries are strings that the library resolves one at a time; call ftsearch in a loop.


8. Logical Soft Deletions
The delete_item! function marks a document as deleted using its internal integer _id. The underlying proximity graph is not restructured:
delete_item!(h, 1)  # Mark internal ID 1 as deleted

results = search(h, query, 5)
first(results).deleted  # Returns true if document 1 is among the top candidates
A query returns such candidates with the field deleted::Bool, so that an application can identify a deleted record without the index being rebuilt.


9. Calibrating Search Hyperparameters: calibrate!
The calibrate! function executes an internal hyperparameter optimization pass over the graph, calibrating BeamSearch parameters across multiple recall thresholds:
calibrate!(h; levels=[0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.97])

# Execute search enforcing minimum 95% target recall
precise_results = search(h, query, 5; minrecall=0.95)
A higher recall target requires more distance computations, and that cost can be measured. Pass a SearchStats instance, and the engine records the cost of that call:
stats = SearchStats()
search(h, query, 5; minrecall=0.8, stats)
cheap = stats.distance_evaluations

search(h, query, 5; minrecall=0.95, stats)
precise = stats.distance_evaluations     # larger: a wider beam examines more of the graph
Over 20,000 random vectors of 32 dimensions, a query for 5 nearest neighbors performs 242 distance computations with minrecall=0.8 and 927 with minrecall=0.95. On that collection, 927 is also the cost of the default beam search, before calibration. An exhaustive scan of the same collection performs 20,000.
Each call overwrites the field; the values are not accumulated, so the field must be read before the next query is issued. ftsearch and the filtered form of search also accept stats. For a filtered search, the reported value is the cost of the candidate search that was executed, not of the k results that satisfied the predicate. An exhaustive backend reports the size of the collection.
This value cannot be obtained in another way. A query uses a context taken from a pool of the engine, and the context returns to the pool when the call ends, so counters read afterwards include the work of any query executed since. The server obtains the distance_evaluations field of its operation log from the same mechanism.


10. Project Closure and Reopening
To close all active RocksDB handles and memory-mapped files:
close_project!(h)
Closing a session that performed writes also compacts the storage of the project. A large insertion leaves a write-ahead log, and the next open must replay it, so the cost appears when the project is opened. On a project of 50,000 vectors, reopening takes 2.97 s without compaction and 0.48 s with it, and the compaction takes 0.16 s. Pass close_project!(h; compact=false) when the closing operation must not be delayed, or call compact_project! after a large insertion, in a process that continues to answer queries.
Reopening the project restores both the stored vectors and graph connectivity:
h2 = open_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense")
reopened_results = search(h2, query, 5)
close_project!(h2)

title: Getting Started
text:
Sparse Vector Search (SparseEngine)
SparseEngine indexes user-provided sparse representations (SparseItem) of fixed dimensionality using an InvertedFile backend.

Indexing Pre-Encoded Sparse Vectors
using SimilaritySearch: Dist
using SparseArrays: sparsevec

const DIM = 1 << 16  # 65,536 dimensions

# Example sparse feature encoder (hashed token frequencies)
function bag_of_words_hash(text::AbstractString)
    counts = Dict{Int32, Float32}()
    for w in split(lowercase(text), r"[^\p{L}\p{N}]+"; keepempty=false)
        k = Int32(mod(hash(w), DIM) + 1)
        counts[k] = get(counts, k, 0.0f0) + 1.0f0
    end
    ind = sort!(collect(keys(counts)))
    val = Float32[counts[i] for i in ind]
    sparsevec(ind, val ./ sqrt(sum(abs2, val)), DIM)  # Unit normalization for NormCosine
end

# Create sparse project
hs = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_sparse";
                    engine=SparseEngine, dimension=DIM, distance=Dist.NormCosine())

# Append sparse items
append_items!(hs, [SparseItem(bag_of_words_hash(it["text"]); doc_id=it["doc_id"], keywords=it["keywords"])
                   for it in items])
index!(hs)  # Idempotent no-op for InvertedFile; items are indexed during append

hits = search(hs, bag_of_words_hash("the monster and its creator"), 5)
for r in hits
    println(r.doc_id, " => Distance: ", round(r.distance; digits=4))
end


Key Properties of SparseEngine

Fixed Dimension Requirement: The dimension parameter must be specified at project creation and must match the coordinate dimension of all appended SparseVector objects.
Strict Query Typing: Queries must be provided as SparseVector{Float32, Int32} matching the configured dimension.
Supported Distance Metrics: Supports Dist.NormCosine over vector weights or discrete set distances (Dist.Sets.Jaccard, Dist.Sets.Dice) over non-zero coordinate supports.

title: Getting Started
text:
Full-Text Retrieval with BM25 (FullTextEngine)
For text retrieval without manual vector encoding, FullTextEngine integrates text normalization, vocabulary management, and inverted file scoring.
using TextSearch: BM25InvertedFile

hb = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_bm25"; 
                    engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
                    textmodel=FitFromCorpus())

# Stage raw text paragraphs
append_items!(hb, [
    TextItem(it["text"]; doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"])
    for it in items[1:200]
])

# First invocation fits the TextProfile and builds the BM25 inverted index
index!(hb)

# Search using natural language queries
hits = ftsearch(hb, "monster creature fear", 5)
for r in hits
    println(r.doc_id, " => Score: ", r.distance)
end

close_project!(hb)
A text project stores the inverted index, not the objects that were indexed, so opening it assembles the index instead of computing it again: 1.4 s against 20.4 s over 265,000 Project Gutenberg paragraphs. This applies to both text backends, BM25 and the weighted TextInvertedFile:
hb2 = open_project(workdir, "frankenstein_bm25")
ftsearch(hb2, "monster creature fear", 5)     # same answers, no reindexing
close_project!(hb2)
Posting lists are read from storage when a query requires them, and are kept in a cache of the most frequently used lists. The size of that cache is set when the project is opened, with postings_cache_max and postings_cache_base: the maximum number of cached lists, and the number the cache is reduced to when the maximum is exceeded. The term vector of each document is read into memory instead, because BM25 computes the score of each candidate from its own vector, and a query that contains a frequent term makes most of the collection a candidate. The architecture guide reports the measurements for both decisions.
A project written by an earlier version stored the indexed objects instead of the index. Such a project opens with no index, and a search against it reports this condition. index!(h) builds the index from the staged text, which was always stored separately. This is the complete migration procedure.
An insertion after the first index! writes only the data that the new block modifies, so a project can grow without being rebuilt. Under FitFromCorpus, however, the vocabulary is determined by the first index!. A word that is absent from the text staged at that moment remains outside the vocabulary, independently of how many blocks are added later. Stage the corpus to be fitted before the first call to index!, or use a BaseProfile.

title: Getting Started
text:
Configuring Linguistic Models (AbstractTextModelSpec)
Text projects require an explicit linguistic model specification passed via the textmodel keyword:

1. DefaultProfile
Loads a published language profile, for example Spanish or English, and refits its vocabulary statistics against the staged corpus during the first call to index!. This is the recommended option when a profile for the language is installed:
hes = create_project(workdir, "news_es"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
                     textmodel=DefaultProfile(:es))
The project then uses the stopword lists, lemma clusters and query-expansion networks derived from a reference corpus, with term frequencies adjusted to the dataset of the project.
The refit keeps most of the vocabulary of the profile. Measured on 2026-09-24 with TextSearch 1.2.1, the Spanish profile holds 730,320 tokens. A refit against 962 paragraphs of Spanish books kept 591,494 of them, and 9,382 of those occur in the paragraphs. A term that the project has not stored yet is therefore usually searchable when a later batch adds it.
The profiles are installed under ~/.textsearch/profiles. TextSearch 1.2 reads profile format 1.1 only. A profile installed with an earlier version of TextSearch is in format 1.0 and does not load. Install it again with download_profile("es"; force=true).


2. FitFromCorpus
Fits a TextProfile directly from the staged corpus without an external reference profile:
using TextSearch: NormalizationConfig

hf = create_project(workdir, "custom_corpus"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
    textmodel=FitFromCorpus(TextConfig(normalization=NormalizationConfig(lc=false, del_diac=false),
                                       language=:es);
                            min_ndocs=3, stopwords=0.9))
The number of documents used for fitting is limited by max_documents, whose default value is 1,000.


3. BaseProfile
Creates a text project from a TextProfile that was computed earlier and read from disk:
hp = create_project(workdir, "wiki_base"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
                    textmodel=BaseProfile(load_profile("wiki-es.zip")))

title: Getting Started
text:
Query Resolution and Expansion: QueryPolicy
A full-text query is executed under a QueryPolicy, which determines the correction of spelling variants and the expansion of the query:
# Default policy: automatic orthographic correction
ftsearch(hes, "musica clasica", 5)

# Disable correction: search literal tokens as entered
ftsearch(hes, "musica clasica", 5; policy=QueryPolicy(correction=:off))

Explaining Corrections: ftexplain
ftexplain reports the token substitutions that were applied to the query:
ftexplain(hes, "musica clasica")


Correcting Misspelled Tokens: edit_correction
The default correction folds case and diacritics, so it maps musica to música. It does not map guerar to guerra, because that correction exchanges two letters. The keyword edit_correction=true adds this kind of correction. A query token that is absent from the vocabulary is replaced by the only vocabulary token at Damerau-Levenshtein distance 1 from it. The Damerau-Levenshtein distance counts insertions, deletions, substitutions and exchanges of two adjacent letters. If there are two or more such tokens, the query token is not replaced.
hes = open_project(workdir, "news_es"; edit_correction=true)
ftexplain(hes, "guerar civil")    # ["guerar not found, searched as guerra (edit) instead"]
The keyword is false by default, and the value is not stored with the project. Each call to open_project or create_project sets it again. QueryPolicy(correction=:off) disables it for one query.
It is disabled by default because it has a cost. The engine builds the edit index from the vocabulary each time it opens the project. Measured on 2026-09-24 over the Spanish profile (730,320 tokens):

title: Getting Started
text:
Full-Text Retrieval with TF-IDF (TextInvertedFile)
To index text using classic TF-IDF weights and cosine distance:
using TextSearch: TextInvertedFile

ht = create_project(workdir, "frankenstein_tfidf"; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=TextInvertedFile,
                    textmodel=FitFromCorpus())

append_items!(ht, [
    TextItem(it["text"]; doc_id = it["doc_id"], keywords = it["keywords"])
    for it in items[1:200]
])
index!(ht)

hits = ftsearch(ht, "monster creature fear", 5)
close_project!(ht)

title: Getting Started
text:
Whole-Dataset Metric Operations
For a dense project with a SearchGraph backend, the package provides algorithms that operate on the entire dataset and execute in the calling process:
h2 = open_project(workdir, "frankenstein_dense")

1. All-Pairs \(k\)-Nearest Neighbors: allknn
Computes the \(k\) nearest neighbors for every indexed element:
neighbors = allknn(h2; k=5)
first(neighbors)  # Returns (id=1, neighbors=[...], dists=[...])


2. Center Selection: fft
Executes the farthest-first traversal to select \(k\) centers that are separated from each other:
R = fft(h2, 8; verbose=false)
R.centers      # Identifiers of the 8 chosen centers
R.separation   # Minimum distance between any two centers
R.covering     # Maximum distance from any object to its assigned center


3. Monochromatic Closest Pairs: closestpairs
Finds the \(k\) closest pairs of objects within the project:
pairs = closestpairs(h2; k=5)
for (i, j, d) in pairs
    ri = get_metadata(h2.project, i)
    rj = get_metadata(h2.project, j)
    println("Pair (", ri.doc_id, ", ", rj.doc_id, ") | Distance: ", d)
end


4. Bichromatic Closest Pairs: bichromatic_kclosestpairs
Finds the \(k\) closest pairs between the indexed project \(A\) and an external matrix collection \(B\):
using SimilaritySearch: MatrixDatabase

second_half_vectors = [vectorize(lsi, it["text"]) for it in items[(half + 1):end]]
B = MatrixDatabase(hcat(second_half_vectors...))

pairs = bichromatic_kclosestpairs(h2, B; k=5)
for (i, j, d) in pairs
    ri = get_metadata(h2.project, i)
    other = items[half + j]
    println("Cross-match (", ri.doc_id, ", ", other["doc_id"], ") | Distance: ", d)
end

title: Getting Started
text:
Metadata Retrieval: fetch_items and exists
To retrieve stored records by internal _id or external doc_id:
# Retrieve full stored record including payload
items_fetched = fetch_items(h2, ["frankenstein_2"])
it = only(items_fetched)
it.doc_id         # "frankenstein_2"
it.keywords       # Indexed keywords array
it.meta           # Free-form metadata dictionary
it.payload        # Stored vector or text

# Check record existence and deletion status
exists(h2, [1, "frankenstein_2", "non_existent_id"])
An external identifier is resolved through a dedicated column family, not by scanning the collection: 0.05 ms against 59 ms for the equivalent scan, measured on a project of 50,000 items. A doc_id is not required to be unique, so fetch_items returns every item that carries the requested identifier, in ascending _id order. The result may therefore contain more elements than the list of identifiers that was given. For the same reason, exists reports an identifier as deleted only when every item that carries it has been deleted.
A numeric argument is first interpreted as an internal _id. It is resolved as a doc_id only when no record has that _id.

title: Getting Started
text:
Summary
This tutorial covered the following operations: 1. Creation of a project with an explicit payload engine and index backend. 2. Insertion with append_items! and construction of the graph or the vocabulary with index!. 3. Nearest-neighbor queries with metadata filtering, an explicit number of candidates, and deleted records. 5. A declared schema for meta, which states what a field holds and how a filter compares it. 4. Batch queries, with metadata (search) or without it (searchbatch). 6. Calibration of the search parameters (calibrate!) for a target recall, and measurement of the cost of a query. 7. Operations over the entire dataset, executed in the calling process. 8. Retrieval by external identifier, and compaction of the storage when the project is closed. 9. Failure handling through the four categories of typed errors.

title: Architecture
text:
Subsystem Architecture and Module Map
The package is structured into four core submodules and an embedded orchestration layer:

Schema: Defines the metadata record contract (Schema.MetadataRecord) and serialization interfaces.
Project: Implements project metadata storage (ProjectManager), document ID indexing, and secondary key lookups.
IndexEngine: Implements the AbstractSearchEngine hierarchy, encapsulating indexing algorithms from SimilaritySearch.jl and TextSearch.jl.
Persistence: Provides storage adapters for RocksDB column families and memory-mapped files.
embedded.jl: Implements EmbeddedEngine and exports the public API (create_project, append_items!, search, and others).






flowchart LR
    Schema["Schema<br/><small>MetadataRecord (_id, doc_id,<br/>keywords, refs), meta JSON</small>"]
    Project["Project<br/><small>ProjectManager, metadata CRUD</small>"]
    IndexEngine["IndexEngine<br/><small>AbstractSearchEngine hierarchy</small>"]
    Persistence["Persistence<br/><small>EngineStore, AdjacencyStore, ...</small>"]
    Embedded["embedded.jl<br/><small>EmbeddedEngine + top-level API</small>"]
    Caller(["Host Julia script, or<br/>SimilaritySearchServer"])

    Schema --> Project
    Schema --> Embedded
    Project --> Embedded
    IndexEngine --> Embedded
    Persistence --> Embedded
    Embedded --> Caller







Decoupling of Subsystems
IndexEngine and Persistence operate independently of Project and Schema: - IndexEngine does not depend on RocksDB. It communicates with persistence only through callbacks of the form (index, sp, ep) -> nothing. - Persistence stores serialized Julia objects through key-value interfaces, and does not interpret the contents of an index. - embedded.jl combines these components into one engine.


Uniform Metadata Contract
Projects use a standardized metadata record structure, Schema.MetadataRecord: - _id: Internal, sequential, zero-based or 1-based integer identifier aligned with vector storage indices. - schema_version: Which declaration of meta was in force when the record was written (see below). - doc_id: Caller-provided external string identifier. - keywords: Indexed string tags mapped via the secondary index idx_keywords. - refs: Indexed document reference links mapped via idx_refs. - meta: Metadata stored as a serialized JSON object, in its own column family.
The record has the same shape in every project. What varies is meta, and a project may declare part of it.


The Declared Shape of meta
A project may declare which fields of meta it expects and what type each one holds. The declaration is a Schema.MetaSchema: a list of (name, type), with the type one of :string, :int64, :float64, :bool or :timestamp.
h = create_project(workdir, "papers"; meta_schema = ["year" => :int64, "published" => :timestamp])
meta_schema(h)                                    # what this project declares
declare_meta_schema!(h, ["year" => :int64])       # declare on a project that exists
append_items! checks each declared field and converts it when the conversion keeps the value: JSON has one number type, so 2024.0 is stored as the integer 2024, and a timestamp is stored as the string its instant prints as. A value of another type raises PayloadMismatch, which is an InvalidRequest.
Three properties define what declaring means here:

It is additive. A field nobody declared is stored as it arrives, and a record need not carry every declared field. Declaring says what a field must hold when it is present, not what an item may contain.
It does not reach backwards. Declaring on a project that already holds records reads none of them. The declaration governs what is written from then on; rebuild is what rewrites the rest. This is what makes declaring cheap on a project of any size.
It is not an index. The declared fields are stored in meta as before, and a filter over them is still evaluated per candidate. What the declaration changes is the comparison: a field declared :timestamp is compared as an instant rather than as the text that stores it, so two spellings of one instant match.

The declaration lives in the project, not in the record: giving MetadataRecord a typed column per declared field would make its Julia type vary from one project to the next, which propagates to every function that handles a record, to the Avro table dump writes, and to a process that holds several projects at once. schema_version on the record is what ties a record to the declaration it was written under.

title: Architecture
text:
Decoupled Lifecycle: Staging vs. Indexing
The package separates the insertion of items from the construction of the index, which is the expensive operation:
[ Ingestion ] ──────> append_items! ──────> [ Staged Backlog ] ──────> index! ──────> [ Searchable Index ]
                     (Durable in Store)                                              (Searchable in Engine)

Behavior of Each Engine Type

SearchGraph (Dense Engine):

append_items! writes the Vector{Float32} arrays to the memory-mapped file dense_vectors.mmapdb. The operation is durable and costs \(O(1)\) per vector. It does not construct graph edges.
index! evaluates the backlog range length(index)+1:length(database(index)) and builds proximity graph connections via SimilaritySearch.index!.

FullTextEngine (Text Engine):

append_items! appends raw text strings to StagedTextStore within RocksDB.
index! processes the staged text backlog:

On the first invocation of an uninitialized project, index! executes the linguistic model specification (fitspec) to build the initial TextProfile and instantiate the inverted index.
On subsequent invocations, index! encodes staged strings and inserts posting list entries.


ExhaustiveSearch and InvertedFile (Sparse Engine):

An exact linear scan evaluates the database directly, and a sparse inverted file updates its posting lists on insertion. append_items! therefore makes an item searchable immediately, and index! performs no work.

title: Architecture
text:
Persistence Architecture
A project is stored in RocksDB column families and in one memory-mapped file. A write modifies only the segments it affects.





flowchart TB
    subgraph db["RocksDB Project Directory"]
        records[("records<br/><small>_id → MetadataRecord</small>")]
        meta[("meta<br/><small>_id → JSON meta blob</small>")]
        oplog[("op_log")]
        idxkw[("idx_keywords<br/><small>keyword → _ids</small>")]
        idxrefs[("idx_refs<br/><small>referenced doc_id → _ids</small>")]
        idxdoc[("idx_docid<br/><small>doc_id → _ids</small>")]
        engine[("engine<br/><small>Field-level engine state</small>")]
        adj[("searchgraph_adj<br/><small>object_id → direct neighbors</small>")]
        stagedtext[("staged_text<br/><small>Raw text blocks</small>")]
        sparsedb[("sparse_db<br/><small>Encoded object blocks</small>")]
        postings[("invfile_postings<br/><small>token → document ids</small>")]
        docvecs[("invfile_docvecs<br/><small>document → indexed vector</small>")]
    end
    mmapfile[["dense_vectors.mmapdb<br/><small>Memory-Mapped Vector File</small>"]]

    ProjectManager -- "Metadata CRUD" --> records
    ProjectManager -- "Unstructured Meta" --> meta
    ProjectManager -- "Secondary Indices" --> idxkw
    ProjectManager -- "Secondary Indices" --> idxrefs
    ProjectManager -- "Secondary Indices" --> idxdoc
    EngineStore -- "save_field! / load_field" --> engine
    AdjacencyStore -- "save_neighbors! / load_neighbors" --> adj
    StagedTextStore -- "append_staged_texts!" --> stagedtext
    InvertedFileObjectStore -- "append_objects!" --> sparsedb
    InvertedIndexStore -- "write_invfile_block!" --> postings
    InvertedIndexStore -- "write_invfile_block! / load_invfile_docvecs" --> docvecs
    append_dense["append_items! (Dense)"] --> mmapfile
    append_text["append_items! (Text)"] --> stagedtext







The Persisted Text Index
A text project stores the index itself: posting lists in invfile_postings, and one vector per document in invfile_docvecs. Both text backends are stored this way. Their posting lists contain the same data, document identifiers, and they differ only in the representation of each document. Three representations are used, and each stored value begins with a one-byte tag that identifies its own: integer term frequencies (BM25), Float32 model weights (the weighted backend), and bags of words (the weighted backend under a set distance, which reads membership instead of weights). A sparse project stores the objects it indexed, in sparse_db, and reconstructs its index at every open. Its items are vectors encoded by the caller, so the stored objects are already the representation that would be written; applying the same treatment to a sparse project remains pending work.
The two procedures differ in cost. Over 265,000 Project Gutenberg paragraphs, reconstruction takes 20.4 s, and assembly from storage takes 1.4 s with BM25 and 1.7 s with the weighted backend (measured 2026-09-11 and 2026-09-12). Indexing the same corpus takes 25.7 s and 26.4 s respectively, compared with 147.3 s before, because a block is now encoded by the parallel batch procedure of the library instead of one document at a time.
Writing is incremental and proceeds by blocks. Each call to index! encodes its backlog as one block, inserts the document vectors and lengths of that block into the index in memory, and passes its posting lists to IndexEngine.persist_block!, with identifiers converted from block-local to global. The implementation of that function reads, modifies and writes one stored list per token that the block contains. Appending is correct because document identifiers increase monotonically: the identifiers of a block are larger than every identifier already stored, so the ascending order required by the merge at query time is preserved. IndexEngine contains no reference to RocksDB, and dispatches on the type of adjacency list of its index.
The unit of writing is the block, and the number of blocks has a cost. The list of a token is rewritten once per block that contains it, so the same 50,000 documents take 5.8 s in one block, 6.8 s in ten, and 10.1 s in fifty (measured 2026-09-12). Large blocks are therefore preferable, which is the result of calling append_items! and then a single index!.
Posting lists are read on demand; document vectors are not. The reason is measured. A query reads one posting list per query term, so reading them from storage increases latency by 1.8% (66.8 ms against 68.0 ms) and removes 55.8 MB of 237.5 MB from memory. Scoring reads the term vector of each candidate (bm25score(..., idx.db[docID])), and the merge makes every document that contains any query token a candidate. With a frequent term, reading document vectors on demand becomes one point read per document in the collection: 1,771.9 ms against 66.8 ms for the same query. Document vectors are therefore read into memory when the project is opened (0.76 s for that corpus).
Posting lists read on demand are kept in a least-frequently-used cache. The cache holds a maximum number of lists and is reduced to a base size when that maximum is exceeded. Lists are removed only after a query has finished, never during one: concurrent searches hold read locks rather than exclusive locks, and a list removed during a query would be read again by any search still using it.
There is no migration from the previous format. A project written before the index was persisted opens with its profile and its staged text, and with no index. A search against it reports this condition, and one call to index! builds the index from the staged text, which was always persisted independently of the index. Supporting the previous format would require keeping the reconstruction procedure for projects that do not yet exist, since no version has been released. The migration is therefore explicit:
h = open_project(workdir, dataset)
index!(h)


External Identifier Resolution
doc_id is the identifier supplied by the caller. It is resolved through the idx_docid column family, not by scanning records. Keys are composite: the bytes of doc_id followed by the four bytes of _id. This allows several items to share one doc_id. fetch_items returns every record that carries the requested identifier, in ascending _id order, and exists reports the identifier as deleted only when all of those records are deleted. On a project of 50,000 items, resolving an external identifier takes 0.12 ms through this index, compared with 59 ms for the scan it replaces.
A project written before this index existed is migrated the first time it is opened for writing. Project.backfill_docid_index! performs one pass over records and writes a marker key, so that later opens do not repeat the pass. A read-only handle opened on a project that has not been migrated uses the scan instead.


Compaction
Bulk writes leave a write-ahead log, and the next open must replay it. Compaction therefore affects the latency of opening a project, not the latency of writing to it. close_project! compacts every column family of the project before closing, unless the handle is read-only, the session performed no writes, or the caller passes compact=false. compact_project! performs the same operation while the project remains open. On a dense project of 50,000 vectors, reopening takes 2.97 s without compaction and 0.28 s with it, and the compaction itself takes 0.03 s.


Storage Subsystems

EngineStore (Engine Field State):

Stores engine-level configuration as individual key-value entries (:minrecall, :opt_beamsearch, :deleted_ids, :profile).
Mutations (e.g., updating deleted IDs or storing calibration results) rewrite only their specific keys.

Dense Vector Storage (dense_vectors.mmapdb):

Dense vectors are stored in a dedicated memory-mapped binary file managed by MMapMatrixDatabase.
Avoids key-value serialization. Appends are sequential, and random access reads the vector without copying it.

AdjacencyStore (Graph Topology):

Graph adjacencies are persisted incrementally through CallbackLog observer hooks during index!.
Stores only forward (direct) edges; reverse edges are reconstructed dynamically in memory during project reopening to ensure idempotency.

StagedTextStore and InvertedFileObjectStore:

StagedTextStore holds un-encoded raw text lines.
InvertedFileObjectStore stores contiguous blocks of encoded posting-list objects.




Project Reopening Lifecycle





sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as open_project
    participant MM as dense_vectors.mmapdb
    participant ES as EngineStore
    participant AS as AdjacencyStore
    participant IE as IndexEngine

    Caller->>ES: load_field(:kind)
    Caller->>MM: Open memory-mapped vector file
    Caller->>ES: load_field(:graph_len)
    Caller->>AS: load_neighbors(i) for i in 1:graph_len
    Caller->>IE: build_searchgraph(distance, vectors, neighbors, graph_len)
    IE->>IE: Restore forward graph adjacencies
    IE->>IE: connect_reverse_links! over 1:graph_len
    IE-->>Caller: Reconstructed DenseEngine{GraphBackend}






When a project is reopened, the stored forward edges are read again and the reverse links are regenerated, which restores the index to the state it had before the project was closed.

section: Dual Logging Architecture: Reporters vs. Observers
text:
Dual Logging Architecture: Reporters vs. Observers
Contexts maintain two isolated logging channels: - Reporters (ctx.reporters): Receive progress messages via INFORM and output formatted status lines to stderr or custom IO streams. Throttled to prevent console flooding. - Observers (ctx.observers): Receive structural mutation events (:add!) via OBSERVE. Execute un-throttled callbacks that trigger persistence updates (CallbackLog).





flowchart LR
    Mutation["append_items! / index!"] --> INFORM["INFORM (ctx.reporters)"]
    Mutation --> OBSERVE["OBSERVE :add! (ctx.observers)"]
    INFORM --> Stderr["InformativeLog → stderr (throttled)"]
    OBSERVE --> CallbackLog["CallbackLog → Persistence Trigger (un-throttled)"]

title: Architecture
text:
Soft Deletions and Dataset Operations

Soft deletions: delete_item! records document identifiers in deleted_ids. The index is not reorganized. A query evaluates such candidates and reports them with the field deleted::Bool of SearchResult.
Operations over an entire collection: allknn, fft, closestpairs and bichromatic_kclosestpairs operate on the index in memory, using multithreaded batch routines over the whole collection.

section: Failure Reporting: Typed Errors and Their Boundaries
text:
Failure Reporting: Typed Errors and Their Boundaries
Every failure that the engine raises is an EngineError. The type of the error, not its message, is the interface. There are four abstract categories, and one or more concrete types under each of them:








category
meaning
concrete types




InvalidRequest
the call cannot be honoured as written; retrying it unchanged fails again
PayloadMismatch, WrongDimension, UnknownBackend, InvalidOption, UnsupportedOperation


NotFound
something the call named does not exist
ProfileNotInstalled


ConflictingState
the request is well formed but the project is not in a state that can serve it; the same call succeeds later
PendingBacklog, NothingStaged, NoIndex, NotTrained, EmptyProject


StorageFailure
what was read back cannot be interpreted
CorruptedStorage



The concrete types carry the values a caller can use. PendingBacklog reports the number of staged items and the number of indexed items, WrongDimension reports the expected and the received length, and InvalidOption reports the keyword that was rejected.
The mapping is defined at each interface, not in the engine. The engine contains no reference to HTTP status codes or to process exit codes. Each consumer performs the translation:
try
    search(handle, query, 10)
catch e
    e isa ConflictingState && return retry_after_indexing()
    e isa NotFound && return not_found()
    rethrow()
end
SimilaritySearchServer maps the categories to status codes: NotFound to 404, ConflictingState to 409, InvalidRequest to 400, and any other failure to 500. Its command lines map the same categories to exit codes 4, 5, 2 and 70, so that a shell script can select a branch without reading the output text. This mapping is the only coupling between the two packages of this repository, and the server manual states it in one table.
The alternative, error("...") with a message, requires every consumer to classify the failure by its text. Such a classification fails when the wording changes, and it fails without any error being reported. This had occurred in this repository: the concurrency test identified a rejected operation with occursin("requires no pending backlog", e.msg). It now matches the type PendingBacklog.

title: Getting Started
text:
Handling Failures
The engine raises typed errors, and the type indicates why the call failed. There are four categories, and a program should select its behavior from the category rather than from the message text:
using SimilaritySearchEngine

try
    searchbatch(h, queries, 10)
catch e
    if e isa PendingBacklog
        # Items were appended but not indexed yet. The engine reports both counts.
        @info "indexing $(e.staged - e.connected) pending item(s) first"
        index!(h)
        searchbatch(h, queries, 10)
    elseif e isa ConflictingState
        rethrow()          # some other state problem: not trained, empty, no index
    else
        rethrow()
    end
end
The categories, and when each one appears:








category
meaning
typical cause




InvalidRequest
the call cannot be honoured as written
a DenseItem appended to a text project, a query of the wrong dimension, dimension on a dense project


NotFound
something the call named does not exist
DefaultProfile(:es) with no profile installed


ConflictingState
the project is not in a state that can serve the request
whole-dataset operations against a staged backlog, ftsearch before the first index!


StorageFailure
stored data this version cannot interpret
a project written by a newer layout



A test against a category matches every concrete type under it. Code written this way continues to work when a new EngineError is added under ConflictingState. A test against a concrete type (PendingBacklog, WrongDimension, InvalidOption) is appropriate when the distinction is required; those types carry the corresponding values: the counts, the expected dimension, and the rejected keyword.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Which half do you need?
Searching inside your own Julia process. The engine is the whole answer: a working directory, a project handle, and function calls. No daemon, no ports, no serialization between you and the index; access control is the file permissions of the working directory.
: Start with Getting started, then Architecture.
Serving search to other processes, machines or languages. The server wraps the same engine in a service: one EmbeddedEngine per dataset, endpoints that translate one request into one engine call, and whole-collection operations dispatched as independent Julia subprocesses so that a query never waits behind an allknn.
: Start with the server tutorial, then the server manual.
Both halves are in one reference, generated from the docstrings: Engine API and Server API.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
What the engine provides

Project Lifecycle Management: Functions create_project, open_project, and close_project! manage the on-disk RocksDB directory and the associated live search engine.
Engine and Backend Separation:

Payload Engines: DenseEngine, SparseEngine, and FullTextEngine specify the stored data domain.
Index Backends: SearchGraph, ExhaustiveSearch, InvertedFile, and BM25InvertedFile define the underlying indexing data structures.
The function payload_kind(engine) identifies the data domain, and the BACKENDS registry enforces valid engine-backend pairings.

Dense Vector Search: Approximate nearest-neighbor search via SearchGraph with dynamic beam-search tuning, or exact brute-force search via ExhaustiveSearch and ParallelExhaustiveSearch. For SearchGraph, insertions (append_items!) and graph construction (index!) are decoupled to give callers explicit control over indexing latency.
Sparse Vector Search: Native inverted index search (InvertedFile) over user-encoded sparse representations of fixed dimension. Distance functions include cosine distance over weights and discrete set metrics (Dist.Sets.*) over non-zero coordinate supports.
Full-Text Retrieval: Lexical search backed by BM25InvertedFile or TF-IDF-weighted TextInvertedFile. The initial index! call fits or initializes a TextProfile from staged texts, establishing the vocabulary and linguistic weighting model.
Explicit Text Modeling: Text projects require an explicit AbstractTextModelSpec:

DefaultProfile(:lang): Resolves a pre-trained language profile and refits vocabulary frequencies against the staged corpus.
BaseProfile(p): Utilizes an existing, pre-computed TextProfile.
FitFromCorpus(cfg): Fits a new profile directly from the staged corpus, bounded by max_documents.
Query execution accepts a QueryPolicy to control automatic orthographic correction and semantic query expansion.

Strongly Typed Interface: Inputs are encapsulated in typed containers (DenseItem, SparseItem, TextItem), and queries return structured results (SearchResult, StoredItem, ExistsResult).
Logical Deletions: The delete_item! function marks documents as logically deleted without mutating the underlying search index. Queries return candidates alongside an explicit deleted flag.
Target Recall Calibration: The calibrate! function executes hyperparameter optimization to calibrate beam-search configurations for target recall constraints (minrecall), and SearchStats reports what a query actually cost in distance computations.
Whole-Dataset Metric Operations: Synchronous, in-process execution of all-pairs nearest neighbors (allknn), diverse center selection (fft), closest pair discovery (closestpairs), and cross-dataset closest pairs (bichromatic_kclosestpairs).
Granular Storage Persistence: High-throughput persistence utilizing a hybrid layout of RocksDB column families and dedicated memory-mapped vector files (dense_vectors.mmapdb).
Typed Errors: Deliberate failures are raised as EngineError subtypes grouped into four categories (InvalidRequest, NotFound, ConflictingState, StorageFailure), so a caller can act on a failure without interpreting its message.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
What the server adds

REST API: dataset lifecycle, append, dense/sparse/text search with metadata filters, soft deletes, recall calibration, and cross-dataset fusion (hybrid, ftsearch_group).
Asynchronous jobs: allknn, fft, neardup, hsp, searchbatch, closestpair, build, dump and load are enqueued and dispatched as independent Julia subprocesses, each opening its dataset read-only so that serving continues while they run.
Two command lines: similarity-search for the data plane against a working directory, similarity-search-ctl for the control plane against a running server — installable as apps with Pkg.Apps.
Operational surface: access tokens, a per-dataset operation log (whose distance-evaluation counts come from the engine’s SearchStats), result cursors for pagination, health and metrics endpoints, and hot unload/reload of a single dataset.
One error vocabulary: the engine’s four categories become HTTP status codes and CLI exit codes by category, never by message — the boundary described above, made concrete.

title: Server Manual
text:
SimilaritySearchServer provides access to SimilaritySearchEngine, the embedded engine documented in the rest of this site, through a REST API, two command lines and an asynchronous job queue. It implements no indexing logic. Storage, indexing and search are implemented in the engine. This package translates HTTP requests and command lines into engine calls, and engine results and failures into responses and exit codes.
This division determines where each subject is documented. Questions about projects, persistence, text profiles or the behavior of a search are answered in the engine’s architecture guide. The two packages are documented on one site because the interface between them is the public API of the engine, and both sides of that interface are described here.

title: Server Manual
text:
1. What this package contains

TOML configuration, and the two ArgParse command lines (similarity-search, similarity-search-admin)

The schema, the persistence layer, the index engine and project management are not part of this package. They are SimilaritySearchEngine.Schema, .Persistence, .IndexEngine and .Project.

title: Server Manual
text:
2. How a dataset is held
The server holds one SimilaritySearchEngine.EmbeddedEngine per dataset identifier, in AppState.handles. That handle contains the two parts of a project, its RocksDB metadata store and its search engine, which keeps them consistent across a restart. reload_datasets! opens every dataset under <workdir>/datasets/ with open_project, and a reopened dataset preserves its index, its text profile, its staged items and its deletion marks.
There is no snapshot file. Earlier versions of this package wrote one JLD2 snapshot per dataset and read it on demand, because the engine did not store its own index. The engine stores it now, and a dataset is the directory that contains it.
A job that operates on an entire dataset runs as a subprocess and opens its project in read-only mode, because the serving process may hold the project open, and the RocksDB write lock is exclusive per process.

A text project is created with FitFromCorpus. Its vocabulary is fitted from the documents the dataset has received when index! is called for the first time. Sending a pre-computed text profile to the server is not available over HTTP.

title: Server Manual
text:
4. REST API (base endpoints)
Every response of this API is JSON. A response that succeeded carries status; one that failed carries error and kind (section 5). The bodies below are real responses, not sketches.
Two names identify an item, everywhere and with one meaning each: doc_id is the identifier the caller gave it, which may be absent, and _id is the integer the engine assigned, which is always there. A search result, a stored record and the operation log all use them that way. Until 2026-09-14 a search result called the first id and the second doc_id, so result.doc_id and record.doc_id were different things; that is corrected, with no alias for the old names.
At the top level of a response, id is the dataset: {"status":"appended","id":"ds"}.

Control

GET /healthz — the process answers HTTP.
GET /readyz — the process is ready to serve. {"status":"ok"}.
GET /metrics — metrics in Prometheus text format: documents and deleted records per dataset, jobs in progress, searches running and waiting, and the counters the operation log feeds — requests per dataset and operation, distance computations, items inserted, and a histogram of request durations.

The counters cover the running process and start at zero when it starts, which is what a Prometheus counter is expected to do; simsearch_process_start_time_seconds reports when that was. They are accumulated as each request is recorded, not read back from the operation log: a collector polls every few seconds, and reading a column family that grows with every request would cost more than the requests it measures. The log remains the durable record and is read through GET /api/v1/datasets/{id}/log.


Datasets

POST /api/v1/datasets — creates one. Accepts id, index_kind (see section 3), distance, dimension, the join-group fields join_group, holds_metadata, key, and an optional meta_schema. Answers 201.
GET /api/v1/datasets?offset=&limit= — every dataset on disk, loaded or not.
GET /api/v1/datasets/{id} — one of them.
DELETE /api/v1/datasets/{id} — destroys it.
POST /api/v1/admin/datasets/{id}/unload and /reload — closes or reopens a dataset without restarting the server. The rebuild subcommand of the command line requires this, because the RocksDB write lock is exclusive per process.

POST /api/v1/datasets          {"status":"created","id":"ds"}
DELETE /api/v1/datasets/{id}   {"status":"deleted","id":"ds"}
POST .../unload                {"status":"unloaded","id":"ds"}
POST .../reload                {"status":"reloaded","id":"ds"}

GET /api/v1/datasets/{id}
{"id":"ds", "index_kind":"searchgraph", "distance":"L2",
 "created_at":"2026-09-14T19:41:57.059", "loaded":true,
 "doc_count":5, "tombstone_count":0, "tombstone_ratio":0,
 "join_group":null, "holds_metadata":false, "key":null,
 "meta_schema":[{"name":"year","type":"int64"}],
 "beamsearch_baseline":{"bsize":4,"delta":1,"maxvisits":1000000}}
GET /api/v1/datasets wraps a list of those objects: {"status":"ok", "datasets":[...], "total":2, "offset":0, "limit":2}. doc_count, tombstone_count, tombstone_ratio, meta_schema and beamsearch_baseline are reported for a dataset that is open; beamsearch_baseline is null for one that is not backed by a graph, and meta_schema is null for one that declares nothing.
meta_schema declares which fields of an item’s metadata the dataset expects and what each one holds:
{"id": "papers", "index_kind": "bm25_invfile",
 "meta_schema": [{"name": "year", "type": "int64"},
                 {"name": "published", "type": "timestamp"}]}
The types are string, int64, float64, bool and timestamp. An append is refused with 400 when a declared field carries another type. Declaring is additive: a field that is not declared is stored as it arrives, and a dataset that declares nothing behaves as before. The declared fields are not indexed; what the declaration changes is that a filter compares in the declared type, so a timestamp is compared as an instant rather than as the text that stores it. The engine holds the declaration inside the project, which is why it survives a restart and travels with dump.

GET /api/v1/datasets/{id}/join_group — the datasets tagged with the same join_group.

{"join_group":"g",
 "members":[{"index_uuid":"txt","index_kind":"bm25_invfile","key":"body","holds_metadata":true}]}


Search and indexing

POST /api/v1/datasets/{id}/append — inserts items. A dense item contains vector, a text item contains text, and a sparse item contains indices and values. The fields doc_id, keywords and refs, and any other field, become the metadata of the item.
POST /api/v1/datasets/{id}/search — dense and sparse search, with optional filter, page_size and beamsearch_overrides.
POST /api/v1/datasets/{id}/ftsearch — text search.
POST /api/v1/datasets/{id}/fetch and GET /api/v1/datasets/{id}/exists?ids= — records by identifier, and whether an identifier exists.
POST /api/v1/datasets/{id}/delete — logical deletion. Takes _id, the integer a search or a fetch reported.
POST /api/v1/datasets/{id}/calibrate — recall calibration for a graph-backed project.
POST /api/v1/search/hybrid and POST /api/v1/search/group — reciprocal rank fusion over two datasets, and a text query sent to every dataset of a join group.

POST .../append     {"status":"appended","id":"ds","inserted":5}
POST .../delete     {"status":"soft_deleted","id":"ds","_id":1}
POST .../calibrate  {"status":"calibrated","id":"ds",
                     "baseline":{"bsize":4,"delta":1,"maxvisits":1000000}}

POST .../search  and  POST .../ftsearch
{"status":"searched","id":"ds",
 "results":[{"doc_id":"d1","_id":1,"distance":0},
            {"doc_id":"d2","_id":2,"distance":1}]}

POST .../fetch
{"status":"fetched","id":"ds",
 "results":[{"doc_id":"d1","_id":1,"keywords":["k1"],"refs":[],
             "schema_version":1,"year":2021}]}

GET .../exists?ids=d1,nope
{"status":"ok","id":"ds",
 "results":[{"id":"d1","doc_id":"d1","_id":1,"exists":true,"deleted":false},
            {"id":"nope","doc_id":null,"_id":null,"exists":false,"deleted":false}]}

POST /api/v1/search/hybrid
{"status":"searched","results":[{"doc_id":"d1","_id":1,"score":0.0327}]}

POST /api/v1/search/group
{"status":"searched","join_group":"g",
 "results":{"body":[{"doc_id":"t1","_id":1,"score":-0.267}]}}
A fetch result merges the item’s metadata into the record, which is why year sits beside keywords above. In exists, id is the string that was asked about, which may be either identifier; doc_id and _id are what it resolved to, and are null when nothing did. A search over a text dataset reports a BM25 score with its sign inverted, under the name distance, which is the convention of the library: a smaller value is a closer match. A filtered search that could not fill k adds "insufficient_results":true, since it reads a bounded number of candidates before applying the filter.
An operation on one dataset is addressed under that dataset. The two queries that read more than one are under /api/v1/search/, which is the only place where a route is not about a single dataset. The earlier prefix /api/v1/simsearch/ was removed on 2026-09-13: it marked a distinction that the API stopped making.


Vocabulary

GET /api/v1/datasets/{id}/vocab?scan=&sample= — what a text dataset’s vocabulary covers.

{"id":"txt", "vocsize":3, "trainsize":3, "numtokens":9, "avgdoclen":3,
 "top_tokens":[{"token":"gato","ndocs":3,"occs":3}],
 "queries":1, "query_tokens":1, "query_oov_tokens":0, "query_oov_rate":0}
With scan=true, six more fields:
{"live_tokens":9, "live_oov_tokens":0, "live_oov_rate":0,
 "live_documents_scanned":3, "live_documents_total":3, "live_sampled":false}
A vocabulary is fitted once and does not grow. The rate over the queries says the words being asked for are missing, and the rate over the documents says the words the dataset already holds are missing; the second is what rebuild corrects, by refitting the vocabulary over the documents the dataset has now.
The query counters cost nothing and are always reported. The reading over the documents is asked for with scan=true, and it is bounded: at most sample documents are read, spread evenly over the dataset, and live_sampled says whether it read all of them. The default sample takes about a second whatever the dataset’s size; sample=0 reads every document, which on a large dataset takes minutes and is better asked for offline with describe. 409 for a dataset that holds no text or was never indexed.


Telemetry

GET /api/v1/datasets/{id}/log?offset=&limit= — the dataset’s op_log: one record per search, ftsearch, append or delete.

{"status":"ok","total":4,"offset":0,"limit":1,
 "entries":[{"operation":"delete","timestamp":"2026-09-14T19:42:11.195",
             "details":{"index_uuid":"ds","_id":1,
                        "user":"alice","token_fingerprint":"703ffec26b6db7b1"}}]}
A search entry carries more in details: distance_name, dimension, distance_evaluations and elapsed_seconds; an append entry carries items_inserted.
user is the name on the token the request carried, and is present when that token was valid. token_fingerprint is the first eight bytes of the token’s SHA-256: enough to tell two tokens of one user apart and to match an entry against a token someone holds, and not enough to present as one. Until 2026-09-14 this field was the token itself, which put live credentials in a column family of the dataset and in every dump of it. The endpoint still requires admin, because the log says who did what, which is an audit surface rather than a reading of the dataset.
The number of distance computations of a search is obtained from the engine, in a SimilaritySearchEngine.SearchStats instance that _run_search passes to search and to ftsearch. It is not obtained by reading a context before and after the call: a search uses a context taken from a pool of the engine, so a counter read from this package includes the work of any other search executed since. For append the second method is correct, because an insertion uses the engine’s own context under an exclusive write lock.


Asynchronous jobs

POST /api/v1/jobs/{kind} — enqueues a job (allknn, fft, neardup, hsp, searchbatch, closestpair, build, dump, load). Answers 202.
GET /api/v1/jobs?offset=&limit=, GET /api/v1/jobs/{job_id} and /result — the jobs, the state of one, and its output.
POST /api/v1/jobs/{job_id}/block, /resume, /kill, and DELETE /api/v1/jobs/{job_id}.
POST /api/v1/admin/jobs/gc — removes the jobs and cursors that have expired.

POST /api/v1/jobs/allknn  [202]   {"status":"accepted","job_id":"fe3198116091f825"}

GET /api/v1/jobs
{"status":"ok","total":1,"offset":0,"limit":1,
 "jobs":[{"id":"fe3198116091f825","kind":"allknn","status":"queued"}]}

POST /api/v1/admin/jobs/gc
{"status":"ok","jobs_purged":[],"cursors_purged":[],"cursors_expired":[]}
A job’s state is queued, running, blocked, completed or failed. GET /api/v1/jobs/{job_id}/result streams the file the job wrote, except for dump, whose result is a directory: for that one it answers {"bundle_dir": ..., "manifest": {...}}.


Tokens

POST /api/v1/admin/tokens — creates one. Accepts user, permissions and an optional expires_at.
GET /api/v1/admin/tokens — every token stored, expired or not.
DELETE /api/v1/admin/tokens/{token} — revokes one.
POST /api/v1/admin/tokens/prune — removes the expired ones.

POST /api/v1/admin/tokens  [201]
{"status":"created","token":"703ffec26b6db7b1...","permissions":["read:*"]}

GET /api/v1/admin/tokens
{"status":"ok",
 "tokens":[{"token":"703ffec26b6db7b1...","user":"alice","permissions":["read:*"],
            "created_at":"2026-09-14T19:42:20.595","expires_at":null}]}

DELETE /api/v1/admin/tokens/{token}   {"status":"revoked"}
POST /api/v1/admin/tokens/prune       {"status":"ok","pruned":0}
The token string is returned once, when it is created. GET /api/v1/admin/tokens is an audit listing and reports them in full, which is why it requires admin.


Authentication
Every /api/v1 endpoint requires a token when [auth] enabled is true in config.toml. /healthz, /readyz and /metrics answer without one, so a supervisor and a metrics collector work without credentials. The default is false, which is the behavior of a server that has never had authentication.
The token travels in the Authorization header, as Bearer <token> or as the bare token. A permission is operation:dataset:








operation
grants
includes




read
the queries and the GET endpoints
—


write
append, delete, calibrate, job submission
read


admin
dataset creation and deletion, the token endpoints, job control, the operation log
write and read



dataset is a dataset id or *. A route that is not about one dataset — listing datasets, the job endpoints, the token endpoints, /api/v1/search/group — requires the operation over *, so a token restricted to one dataset uses that dataset and cannot enumerate the rest. admin:* grants everything. A request without a valid token is answered 401; a valid token without the permission is answered 403, and the body names the permission that was required.
The first token is created against the working directory, because a server with authentication enabled refuses to start while no token exists, and the endpoint that creates tokens is itself behind authentication:
similarity-search add-token --user admin --permissions "admin:*" --workdir ./workdir
Later tokens are created with POST /api/v1/admin/tokens or with similarity-search-ctl add-token, which is the same endpoint. A token may carry an expires_at, an ISO 8601 timestamp that is verified when the token is created and again on every request.

text:
5. How failures are reported
The engine raises typed errors. This package maps them by category, never by the text of the message:








engine category
HTTP
CLI exit code




NotFound
404
4


ConflictingState (staged backlog, untrained profile, empty project)
409
5


InvalidRequest (wrong payload, wrong dimension, bad option)
400
2


StorageFailure
500
70



Two status codes come from this package rather than from the engine: 401 when a request carries no valid token, and 403 when its token lacks the permission the route requires.
An error response contains two fields: error, the message, intended for a person, and kind, the concrete engine type, intended for a client that selects a behavior. Failures detected by a command line itself, such as a dataset directory that does not exist or an input file that cannot be read, return exit code 1. They are detected before the engine is called.

title: Server Manual
text:
6. Configuration
config.toml (or .similarity-search-server.toml):
[paths]
workdir = "./workdir"

[server]
host = "127.0.0.1"
port = 8080

[resources]
query_threads_pct = 80
batch_threads_pct = 20
max_concurrent_queries = 0
max_concurrent_queries bounds how many searches run at once. 0 derives it from the split below: the threads that job execution did not reserve. A request that arrives when every slot is taken waits for one; it is not refused, because a caller that asked for a search wants the search. /metrics reports simsearch_queries_running, simsearch_queries_waiting, simsearch_query_slots and simsearch_query_wait_seconds_total, which is what says whether the bound is ever reached.
The bound exists because unbounded concurrency buys no throughput and does cost memory. Past the number of threads, more concurrent searches share the same cores and each one gets slower; and every concurrent search holds a context from the engine’s pool, which grows to the highest concurrency ever reached and does not shrink.
The same split governs the work that runs inside this process rather than in a job. Indexing and calibration divide their work into batches, one task each, and the engine takes the batch count from the number of threads; this server caps it at the share reserved for batch work, so that an append that triggers index! does not spread over the threads answering queries. A job needs no such cap: it is a subprocess started with its share in JULIA_NUM_THREADS. serve prints both numbers when it starts. PLAN.md §2 proposed a request collector for this: a channel and a pool of worker tasks that every search would pass through. This is the bound without that structure, and the measurements a collector would be justified by are the ones above.
[resources] divides this server’s threads between answering queries and executing jobs. A job runs as its own process, so the reserved share is spent as a number of processes and a number of threads each: at most four jobs at once, each with its part of floor(threads × batch_threads_pct / 100), and never more than that share in total. The remaining threads stay with the server. serve prints the resulting numbers when it starts, for example at most 4 concurrent job(s), 3 thread(s) each (20.0% of this server's 64 thread(s)).
The number of threads the server itself has is the one given to Julia when it starts (julia -t auto), not a value in this file.

title: Server Manual
text:
7. Tests
Two levels, selected with test_args=["full"] or SSE_TEST_LEVEL=full:

light (50 assertions, approximately 5 s): the interface with the engine. It verifies the mapping from the names used in requests to engine types, from engine errors to status codes and exit codes, and from the items of a request to engine items. No server is started and no subprocess is created. This level detects a change in the engine on the day it is made.
full (585 assertions, approximately 19 minutes): the end-to-end suites for the API, the jobs and the command lines. They start servers and execute subprocesses. Near the end, the run produces no output for about ten minutes, while the command-line suite waits for jobs to expire. The run has not stopped.

julia --project=server -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.develop(path="."); Pkg.test()'
julia --project=server -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.test(test_args=["full"])'
