title: Server Tutorial
text:
This tutorial starts the server, creates a dataset, indexes documents, searches them, and executes an asynchronous job. It assumes a local copy of this repository. SimilaritySearchServer is the package in server/, and the engine it uses is the package at the root, whose tutorial is Getting started.
Every operation below is performed over HTTP or from a command line, and none of them is implemented in this package: each endpoint translates one engine call. Reading both tutorials together shows which part performs each operation.
Julia 1.12 or later is required.

title: Server Tutorial
text:
Step 1: Set up the environment
The server uses the engine from this repository, so the engine is added by path once:
julia --project=server -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.develop(path="."); Pkg.instantiate()'

title: Server Tutorial
text:
Step 2: Start the server
julia --project=server -t auto -m SimilaritySearchServer serve
On its first execution, the server writes a default configuration and accepts connections on http://127.0.0.1:8080. Every dataset is stored under <workdir>/datasets/, and the server opens all of them when it starts, so a restart preserves their contents.
The three applications (similarity-search, similarity-search-admin, similarity-search-serve) can be installed into ~/.julia/bin, so that Julia does not have to be invoked explicitly:
julia -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.Apps.develop(path="server")'

title: Server Tutorial
section: Step 3: Create a dataset and index documents
text:
Step 3: Create a dataset and index documents
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/datasets \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"id": "demo", "index_kind": "bm25_invfile"}'

curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/datasets/demo/append \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"items": [
           {"doc_id": "d1", "text": "el gato duerme sobre el tejado", "keywords": ["gato"]},
           {"doc_id": "d2", "text": "un perro ladra en la calle", "year": 2024}
         ]}'
index_kind names the type of data the project holds and the structure that indexes it: searchgraph for dense vectors, which is the default; bm25_invfile or invfile for text; and sparse_invfile for sparse vectors encoded by the caller, which also requires dimension. Any field other than doc_id, keywords, refs, text, vector, indices and values becomes metadata of the item, such as year in the example above.
The insertion indexes the documents, so they can be searched when the call returns.

title: Server Tutorial
text:
Step 4: Search
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/datasets/demo/ftsearch \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"text": "gato tejado", "k": 5}'
A dense project uses /api/v1/datasets/{id}/search, which receives a vector and accepts a metadata filter:
{"vector": [0.1, 0.2, 0.3], "k": 10, "filter": {"year": {"$gte": 2024}}}
A filtered search reads a limited number of candidates before applying the filter, so it can return fewer than k results. The response reports this condition in the field insufficient_results.

Step 5: Read failures
Failures are typed, and the status code identifies the class of the failure without the message being read:

the request cannot be executed as written

The body contains error, the message, and kind, the concrete error type of the engine, so that a client can select a behavior from kind without comparing text.

title: Server Tutorial
text:
Step 6: Run a heavy job
An operation that reads the entire collection is executed as a job. The HTTP call enqueues the job and returns immediately, and a dispatcher executes it in a separate Julia subprocess.
JOB=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/jobs/allknn \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"dataset": "demo", "k": 5}' | jq -r .job_id)

curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/jobs/$JOB          # queued | running | completed | failed
curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/jobs/$JOB/result   # once completed
A job opens its dataset in read-only mode, so it can run while the server continues to answer queries on that dataset.

title: Server Tutorial
section: Step 7: The same thing from the command line
text:
Step 7: The same thing from the command line
Every operation is also available as a subcommand, applied to a working directory instead of a URL:
julia --project=server -m SimilaritySearchServer build \
      --dataset demo_cli --input corpus.jsonl --index-kind bm25_invfile --workdir ./workdir

julia --project=server -m SimilaritySearchServer describe --dataset demo_cli --workdir ./workdir
The exit codes of the command line correspond to the status codes above: 2 for an invalid request, 4 for an object that does not exist, 5 for a conflicting state, and 70 for a storage failure. Code 1 is reserved for failures detected by the command itself, such as a dataset that does not exist or an input file that cannot be read. A script can select a branch from these codes without reading the output.

title: Server Tutorial
text:
Step 8: The Python client
cd server/python
pip install -r requirements.txt
export PYTHONPATH=$(pwd)
from similarity_search.client import SimilaritySearchClient
from similarity_search.jobs import run_job

client = SimilaritySearchClient("http://127.0.0.1:8080")
print(client.readyz())                      # {'status': 'ok'}

ds_id = client.create_dataset()
result = run_job(client, kind="allknn", command=["--dataset", ds_id, "--k", "5"])
stress_client.py executes the same sequence under concurrent load:
python stress_client.py --jobs 3

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Choosing a package
To search within a Julia process, use the engine. It requires a working directory, a project handle, and function calls. No server process, network port or serialization is involved. Access control is provided by the file permissions of the working directory.
: Begin with Getting started, then read Architecture.
To provide search to other processes, machines or programming languages, use the server. It holds one EmbeddedEngine per dataset, and translates each request into one engine call. An operation over an entire collection is executed in a separate Julia subprocess, so that a query is not delayed by a long operation such as allknn.
: Begin with the server tutorial, then read the server manual.
Both packages are documented in one generated reference: Engine API and Server API.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Engine functionality

Project lifecycle: create_project, open_project and close_project! manage the on-disk RocksDB directory and the associated search engine.
Separation of engine and backend:

Payload engines: DenseEngine, SparseEngine and FullTextEngine determine the type of data stored.
Index backends: SearchGraph, ExhaustiveSearch, InvertedFile and BM25InvertedFile determine the indexing data structure.
payload_kind(engine) reports the data type, and the BACKENDS registry restricts which engine-backend pairs are valid.

Dense vector search: approximate nearest neighbor search with SearchGraph, which tunes its beam search parameters, or exact search with ExhaustiveSearch and ParallelExhaustiveSearch. For SearchGraph, insertion (append_items!) and graph construction (index!) are separate operations, so the caller determines when indexing latency is incurred.
Sparse vector search: inverted index search (InvertedFile) over sparse representations encoded by the caller, of fixed dimension. The available distance functions are cosine distance over the weights and set distances (Dist.Sets.*) over the support of the non-zero coordinates.
Full-text retrieval: lexical search with BM25InvertedFile or with TF-IDF weighting (TextInvertedFile). The first call to index! fits or initializes a TextProfile from the staged texts, which determines the vocabulary and the term weighting model.
Explicit text modeling: a text project requires an AbstractTextModelSpec:

DefaultProfile(:lang) resolves a pre-trained language profile and refits the vocabulary frequencies against the staged corpus.
BaseProfile(p) uses an existing TextProfile.
FitFromCorpus(cfg) fits a profile from the staged corpus, up to max_documents.
A query accepts a QueryPolicy, which determines orthographic correction and query expansion.
edit_correction=true, given to create_project or open_project, also corrects a query token that is absent from the vocabulary when exactly one vocabulary token is at edit distance 1 from it.

Typed interface: input is given in typed containers (DenseItem, SparseItem, TextItem), and queries return structured results (SearchResult, StoredItem, ExistsResult).
Logical deletion: delete_item! marks a document as deleted without modifying the index. Queries return such candidates with an explicit deleted field.
Recall calibration: calibrate! optimizes the beam search parameters for a set of target recall values, which minrecall then selects. SearchStats reports the number of distance computations a query performed.
Operations over an entire collection: in-process execution of all-pairs nearest neighbors (allknn), center selection (fft), closest pairs (closestpairs), and closest pairs between two collections (bichromatic_kclosestpairs).
Persistence: RocksDB column families for metadata and index structures, and memory-mapped files for dense vectors (dense_vectors.mmapdb).
Typed errors: a failure raised by the engine is an EngineError in one of four categories (InvalidRequest, NotFound, ConflictingState, StorageFailure), so that a caller can act on a failure without interpreting its message.

title: SimilaritySearchEngine.jl
text:
Server functionality

REST API: dataset lifecycle, insertion, dense, sparse and text search with metadata filters, logical deletion, recall calibration, and queries over more than one dataset (hybrid, ftsearch_group).
Asynchronous jobs: allknn, fft, neardup, hsp, searchbatch, closestpair, build, dump and load are enqueued and executed as separate Julia subprocesses. Each one opens its dataset in read-only mode, so the server continues to answer queries while they run.
Two command lines: similarity-search operates on a working directory, and similarity-search-ctl operates on a running server over HTTP. Both can be installed as applications with Pkg.Apps.
Operational interfaces: access tokens, an operation log per dataset (whose distance-computation counts are obtained from the engine’s SearchStats), cursors for paginated results, health and metrics endpoints, and unload and reload of a single dataset without restarting the server.
One error vocabulary: the engine’s four categories are mapped to HTTP status codes and to command-line exit codes by category, not by message text.

title: Architecture
text:
Logging Channels: Reporters and Observers
A context maintains two separate logging channels: - Reporters (ctx.reporters): Receive progress messages via INFORM and output formatted status lines to stderr or custom IO streams. Throttled to prevent console flooding. - Observers (ctx.observers): Receive structural mutation events (:add!) via OBSERVE. Execute un-throttled callbacks that trigger persistence updates (CallbackLog).





flowchart LR
    Mutation["append_items! / index!"] --> INFORM["INFORM (ctx.reporters)"]
    Mutation --> OBSERVE["OBSERVE :add! (ctx.observers)"]
    INFORM --> Stderr["InformativeLog → stderr (throttled)"]
    OBSERVE --> CallbackLog["CallbackLog → Persistence Trigger (un-throttled)"]

title: Multilingual Paragraph Search over Books and Wikipedia
text:
Dataset Preparation
The datasets and the text profiles used in this tutorial are produced by tutorials/prepare.jl. The script downloads texts in the public domain, divides them into paragraphs, fits the text profiles, and indexes the corpora:
# Complete build (approximately one hour)
julia -t 8 --project=tutorials tutorials/prepare.jl

title: Multilingual Paragraph Search over Books and Wikipedia
text:
Linguistic Profiles (TextProfile)
A text project requires a TextProfile, which defines the tokenization of the vocabulary, the term weighting, the stopword list, the lemma map, and the query-expansion network.
The preparation script fits the profiles with the procedure of TextSearch.jl (textsearch fit). That procedure applies Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) to obtain word embeddings, and builds the query-expansion structures from them.

Normalization Policy: Preserving Case and Diacritics
The corpora are processed under the following normalization configuration:
[normalization]
del_diac = false      # Preserve diacritical marks (e.g., accents)
lc = false            # Preserve character casing
del_punc = true       # Remove punctuation marks
group_num = true      # Normalize numeric sequences
group_url = true      # Normalize URL strings
Preserving case and diacritics preserves distinctions in meaning, for example between a proper noun and a common noun, or between two words of a Romance language that differ only in an accent. The query is resolved against this vocabulary, and a query written without accents is mapped to the accented form at search time.

Orthographic Query Correction
Because linguistic profiles preserve diacritics, unaccented search terms (e.g., musica) do not match accented vocabulary entries (música) by default.
Under the default QueryPolicy(correction=:auto), the query resolution engine identifies unaccented query terms and maps them to their most probable accented vocabulary counterparts:


Query: la musica del corazon
  ~ musica is in 9 documents against música's 724, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as música (variant), Música (variant) instead

Query: el pais y la republica
  ~ republica is in 3 documents against República's 307, so it reads as a misspelling; searched as República (variant), república (variant) instead



ftexplain reports the token substitutions that were applied. A query written with correct orthography produces no substitution:


ftexplain output on correctly typed query: String[]

title: Multilingual Paragraph Search over Books and Wikipedia
text:
Programmatic Project Lifecycle
The following example performs the complete sequence over a subset of one corpus:
# 1. Ingest slice of paragraph records
slice = map(Iterators.take(eachline(corpus_file("gutenberg-en")), 2000)) do line
    o = JSON3.read(line)
    meta = Dict{String,Any}(String(k) => v for (k, v) in pairs(o) if k !== :text && k !== :doc_id)
    SSE.TextItem(String(o.text); doc_id=String(o.doc_id), meta)
end

# 2. Create project using a pre-computed BaseProfile
workdir = mktempdir()
h = SSE.create_project(workdir, "sample_project";
        engine    = SSE.FullTextEngine,
        backend   = TextSearch.BM25InvertedFile,
        textmodel = SSE.BaseProfile(profiles["gutenberg-en"]))

# 3. Stage items (durable on disk, pending indexing)
SSE.append_items!(h, slice)

# 4. Construct inverted file postings over staged backlog
quiet() do
    SSE.index!(h)
end

# 5. Execute full-text query
results = SSE.ftsearch(h, "the whale", 3)

Performance Observations

Cost of persistence: writing each document to RocksDB adds little time compared with an indexing loop in memory, and the data survive an interruption of the process.
Compilation time: the first execution in Julia includes the compilation of the code. Later batches show the rate of the compiled code.
Storage of the profile: creating a project with a fitted profile writes that profile into the RocksDB store of the project, so the project can be copied to another machine without additional files.
Storage of the index: a text project stores the inverted index, so opening it does not index the corpus again. The architecture guide reports the difference: 1.4 s against 20.4 s for the largest of these corpora.

title: Server Tutorial
text:
Step 9: Require a token
Everything above answered without credentials, which is the default. To require a token on every /api/v1 endpoint, create the first token against the working directory and enable authentication:
similarity-search add-token --user admin --permissions "admin:*" --workdir ./workdir
[auth]
enabled = true
The command prints the token once. A server started with enabled = true and no token refuses to start, because no request could be answered. From then on, each request carries it:
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/datasets/demo/ftsearch \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"text": "gato tejado", "k": 5}'
A permission is operation:dataset, with read, write or admin as the operation and a dataset id or * as the scope. A token for an ingestion process is --permissions "write:demo", which also reads demo and reaches nothing else. /healthz, /readyz and /metrics keep answering without a token. See the server manual for the complete table.

title: Getting Started
section: What the Vocabulary Does Not Cover
text:
What the Vocabulary Does Not Cover
A text project fits its vocabulary once, from the documents staged when index! first ran. A word that vocabulary does not contain cannot be searched for: it is dropped when a query is encoded, and dropped again when a document that contains it is indexed. vocabulary_report measures how much of that is happening:
report = vocabulary_report(hb)
report["vocsize"]            # how many tokens the vocabulary holds
report["queries"]            # queries answered since the project was created
report["query_oov_rate"]     # of the tokens they carried, the fraction it did not have
The query counters are accumulated as queries arrive, at the cost of tokenizing each query string, and they are stored in the project: closing and reopening it does not reset them.
The second reading costs a pass over the project and is asked for explicitly:
scanned = vocabulary_report(hb; scan=true)
scanned["live_oov_rate"]     # of the tokens in the stored documents, the fraction missing
The two answer different questions, and the difference decides what to do:

A high rate over the queries says people are asking for words this project does not index. If those words are not in the documents either, no rebuild helps: the corpus does not contain what is being asked for.
A high rate over the documents says the project stores words its vocabulary does not have, which happens to any project that keeps growing after its first index!. That is what rebuild corrects, by refitting the vocabulary over the documents that are there now.
